topics.title: Gemini Studios and the make-up room

learn.hook: Make-up bought by the truckload, a room once said to be a British general's stables, and lights hot enough to fry an actor. Welcome to Gemini Studios.
points: Author: Asokamitran, a Tamil writer who worked at Gemini Studios, Madras, from 1952 to the mid-1960s. The chapter is an extract from his memoir 'My Years with Boss'.
Tone: a humorous memoir. 'The Boss' is S.S. Vasan, the founder of Gemini Studios.
Pancake: the brand of make-up material that Gemini Studios bought by the truckload for its actors.
The make-up department was upstairs in a building said to have been Robert Clive's stables.
Incandescent lights and large mirrors made it like a hair-cutting salon turned torture chamber; the heavy make-up turned decent-looking actors into crimson-hued monsters.

steps: 'Pancakes' refers to Pancake, the make-up brand used at Gemini.
'Poets' refers to the many poets and writers who worked there, like Subbu.
Together they sum up the studio: glamour and literature side by side.
example.answer: Pancake is the make-up brand; poets are the studio's writers. The title captures the two worlds of Gemini Studios.

learn.reallife: Today's film sets in Hyderabad's Ramoji Film City or Mumbai's Film City still have make-up vans and hot lights, but cooler LED lighting has made the 'torture chamber' far gentler.

topics.title: National integration and the frustrated office boy

learn.hook: A Bengali, a Maharashtrian, a Kannadiga, an Andhra, an Anglo-Burmese and local Tamils, all in one make-up room. The author calls it 'national integration', with a wink.
points: The make-up department showed 'national integration': a Bengali chief (later succeeded by a Maharashtrian), with a Dharwar Kannadiga, an Andhra, a Madras Indian Christian, an Anglo-Burmese and local Tamils.
Strict hierarchy: the chief made up the main actors, his assistants the lesser players, and the office boy the crowd players.
The office boy, in his early forties, had joined the studio hoping to become a star actor, screenwriter, director or lyricist. He was a bit of a poet, but stayed in a dead-end job.
Frustrated, he blamed Kothamangalam Subbu, the No. 2 at Gemini, for his failure and poured out his anger to the author.

example.q: How does the author create humour with the phrase 'national integration'?
steps: National integration is a grand political ideal.
He applies it to a small, noisy make-up room.
The mismatch between the big phrase and the small setting is funny.
example.answer: By using a serious national ideal to describe a mixed group of make-up men; the mock-grand phrase is humorous.

learn.reallife: Indian film crews today still bring together people from every state. A single Bollywood or Tollywood set may hear five languages before lunch.

learn.hook: One man is cheerful, loyal and endlessly creative. Another, nicknamed 'the opposition', ends a career with a tape recorder.
points: Kothamangalam Subbu: the No. 2 at Gemini, a poet and the Boss's loyal aide; always cheerful, and able to suggest many ways of shooting a scene.
He wrote poetry and the novel 'Thillana Mohanambal', acted well, and supported many dependants with great generosity.
The legal adviser, nicknamed 'the opposition' by others, was the only one in pants, tie and sometimes a coat, while others wore khadi.
He once secretly recorded an actress's angry outburst on the set and played it back to her; she was stunned into silence, and her career ended.

example.q: Why was the legal adviser called 'the opposition'?
steps: A legal adviser should help the studio.
Instead, his actions, like taping the actress, harmed the studio's work.
So, ironically, he worked like the opposition.
example.answer: Because instead of helping, he often created problems, as when he ended a talented actress's career.

learn.reallife: Many Indian film studios have had creative all-rounders like Subbu: writer, lyricist and actor in one. Tamil cinema still celebrates such multi-talented artists.

topics.title: Clippings, a closed department and the MRA visit

learn.hook: The author's job was cutting newspapers. Everyone thought he did nothing. Then two hundred foreigners arrived to stage plays.
points: The author's job was to cut out newspaper clippings on many subjects and file them. Because he sat in a cubicle with scissors and paper, others thought he did nothing.
The Story Department of writers and poets was eventually closed, and the legal adviser, part of it, lost his job too.
Gemini Studios was anti-communist; most of its people wore khadi and admired Gandhi. The Boss welcomed the Moral Re-Armament Army (MRA), an international anti-communist group, in 1952.
About two hundred MRA members staged the plays 'Jotham Valley' and 'The Forgotten Factor'. Tamil drama later copied their sunrise and sunset scenes.

example.q: Why did people think the author did nothing?
steps: His work was quiet: cutting and filing newspapers.
He sat alone in a cubicle with scissors.
Others assumed this was not real work.
example.answer: His quiet job of cutting newspaper clippings looked to others like idleness, so they came to him to pour out their troubles.

learn.reallife: Research teams in Indian newsrooms still keep 'clippings libraries'. What looked like 'nothing' to Gemini staff is the backbone of good research.

learn.hook: An English poet gives a long speech to a Tamil film studio. Nobody understands a word, and nobody knows who he is.
points: An English poet visited Gemini Studios and spoke to the staff. His accent and subject were beyond them; nobody understood him, and why he had come remained a mystery.
Years later the author found out: the visitor was Stephen Spender, the English poet and editor of the magazine 'The Encounter'.
Spender was one of the contributors to 'The God That Failed', essays by former communists: André Gide, Richard Wright, Ignazio Silone, Arthur Koestler, Louis Fischer and Spender himself.
The episode shows the cultural gap between an English poet and Tamil film workers, and the anti-communist mood of the era.

example.q: Why was the poet's visit a 'mystery'?
steps: Tamil film workers could not follow his English or his ideas about poetry.
A poet had no clear link with a studio making Tamil films.
So no one knew who he was or why he came.
example.answer: His speech made no sense to the audience, and his purpose at a Tamil film studio was never clear.

learn.reallife: International writers still visit Indian festivals like the Jaipur Literature Festival. Today, translators and subtitles help bridge the gap that left Gemini's staff baffled.

learn.hook: Asokamitran never tells a joke. He just describes things with a straight face, and that is what makes them funny.
points: Humour, irony and gentle satire on the film industry: hot lights that make actors into monsters, a 'national integration' of make-up men.
Self-deprecating humour: the author laughs at himself, calling his job one that others thought was doing nothing.
Irony and understatement: the legal adviser called 'the opposition'; a lawyer losing his job because poets were sent home.
Mock-heroic description: small matters told in grand language, such as Clive's stables or national integration.
Anecdotal structure: the chapter is a chain of anecdotes; characters like the office boy, Subbu and the legal adviser are drawn almost as caricatures.

example.q: Identify the device: 'The make-up department was said to have been Robert Clive's stables.'
steps: A great historical name is attached to a humble room.
The grand reference makes the ordinary setting look funny.
This is mock-heroic humour mixed with irony.
example.answer: Mock-heroic irony: a lofty historical reference used for an ordinary make-up room.

learn.reallife: Indian comic writers like R.K. Laxman, in his cartoons, used the same straight-faced irony to poke fun at offices and officials.

topics.title: Board exam practice: Poets and Pancakes

learn.hook: Subbu, the MRA and Spender: three short-answer favourites. One long answer on humour. Let's lock them in.
points: Think as you read: Pancake is the make-up brand; the office boy was a frustrated would-be star; the author was thought to do nothing because he cut newspapers.
Understanding: humour through irony, exaggeration and self-mockery; Subbu as a many-sided genius (poet, novelist, actor, generous friend); the legal adviser who ended an actress's career.
The poet's visit was a mystery because no one understood him; 'The God That Failed' was a book of essays by ex-communists, including Spender.
Discussion: humour as a tool to criticise gently; the place of poetry and lyrics in Indian films.
Long answer on humour: give at least three examples, such as Clive's stables, 'national integration', the 'opposition' nickname and the do-nothing author.

learn.reallife: Tamil cinema has a long tradition of poet-lyricists, from Kannadasan to Vairamuthu, showing that poetry and film often share a stage.
